blocks.title: The League and mandates
blocks.md: The **League of Nations** was set up after the First World War (1920) to keep peace. Former German and Ottoman colonies were placed under the **mandate system**: a victorious power administered the territory on behalf of the League as a ‘sacred trust’ for the people’s well-being. Mandates were grouped as A, B and C according to their supposed readiness for self-rule. Cameroon and Togo were **B mandates**.

blocks.title: Supervision
blocks.md: Mandatory powers sent annual reports to the **Permanent Mandates Commission** of the League. In principle they had to protect inhabitants’ interests, prevent abuses such as slavery and promote welfare. In practice the League had little power, and the mandatory powers governed in much the same way as their other colonies.

blocks.caption: From League mandates to UN trusteeship.
blocks.alt: A table of the League, the UN and the mandates with approximate years and roles.

blocks.title: In Cameroon
blocks.md: France governed **French Cameroun** from Yaoundé (as a separate territory) and Britain administered **Northern and Southern Cameroons** as part of Nigeria. Both kept up plantations and cash-crop exports, built roads and schools through missions and government, and used taxes and labour requirements.

blocks.title: Be accurate
blocks.md:
- Mandates did not mean independence, and the League did not rule the territories directly.
- ‘B mandate’ is a classification in the League system, not a type of colony.
- Do not confuse the League of Nations (1920) with the United Nations (1945).

blocks.title: Example 1 — The aim of the mandate
blocks.statement: State two aims of the mandate system.
steps: To administer former colonies for the well-being of their inhabitants.
To supervise the powers through reports and the Permanent Mandates Commission.
blocks.answer: Welfare as a ‘sacred trust’ and international supervision.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Limits of the system
blocks.statement: Explain two weaknesses of the mandate system.
steps: The League could not enforce its decisions and relied on annual reports.
Mandatory powers ran the territories much as their colonies, with limited African participation.
blocks.answer: Weak supervision and little change in practice.

blocks.title: Indirect rule
blocks.md: **Indirect rule**, associated with Frederick Lugard in Nigeria, governed through existing African rulers, called **Native Authorities**, supervised by British officials. It was cheap, since few officials were needed, and kept some traditional institutions, but it gave power to some chiefs, created chiefs where none existed, and limited modern change.

blocks.title: Direct rule and assimilation
blocks.md: French rule was more **direct**: a governor and district officers (*commandants*), with chiefs used as agents of the administration. The policy of **assimilation** aimed to make a small educated elite French in language and culture. Africans under the *indigénat* code were subject to special penalties and labour duties.

blocks.caption: British and French colonial approaches compared.
blocks.alt: A three-column table comparing approach, chiefs and aim for British and French colonial rule.

blocks.title: Comparison
blocks.md: Both systems aimed to control territory, tax, and organise the export of raw materials. British rule left more space for local rulers and for local languages, while French rule promoted the French language and centralised power. In practice the differences were not absolute: both used chiefs and both used force.

blocks.title: Do not overgeneralise
blocks.md:
- British rule was not always ‘indirect’: where there were no strong chiefs the system was harder to apply.
- French assimilation reached few Africans: most were not citizens.
- Treat the labels as tools, not as exact descriptions of each place.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Advantage and disadvantage
blocks.statement: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of indirect rule.
steps: Advantage: cheap and kept local institutions.
Disadvantage: concentrated power in chiefs who might misuse it, and slowed the development of new forms of representation.
blocks.answer: Cost saving versus abuse and limited change.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Comparison
blocks.statement: Compare the language policies of British and French rule.
steps: Britain allowed local languages in primary schooling and used English for higher levels.
France promoted French in schools and government.
Both created elites using the colonial language.
blocks.answer: British: more local languages; French: assimilation through French.

blocks.title: The UN
blocks.md: The **United Nations** was founded in **1945**, after the Second World War, to maintain peace and security, promote human rights and encourage cooperation. Its Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 and came into force in October 1945. Main organs: **General Assembly**, **Security Council** (five permanent members with a veto), **Secretariat**, **International Court of Justice**, **Economic and Social Council** and the **Trusteeship Council**.

blocks.title: Trusteeship
blocks.md: The UN replaced League mandates with **trusteeship** for former mandates and some other territories. Administering powers had to promote the political, economic and social progress of the inhabitants towards **self-government or independence**, and report to the Trusteeship Council, which sent **visiting missions**. In **1946** the British and French Cameroons became trust territories.

blocks.caption: Main organs of the United Nations.
blocks.alt: Six boxes naming the six main UN organs.

blocks.title: Impact on decolonisation
blocks.md: The UN gave a forum where anti-colonial views were heard, and the General Assembly passed the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples in 1960. UN supervision, visiting missions and petitions gave Cameroonians a way to raise their demands, and UN plebiscites in 1961 settled the future of the British Cameroons.

blocks.title: Don’t confuse
blocks.md:
- UN Trusteeship (1946) replaced the League’s mandates; the administering powers were the same.
- Trusteeship aimed at self-government or independence; mandates had a vaguer aim.
- The Security Council’s five permanent members are not elected: they hold a veto.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Change from mandate to trusteeship
blocks.statement: State two differences between mandates and trusteeship.
steps: Trusteeship had the explicit aim of self-government or independence.
It was supervised by the Trusteeship Council with visiting missions and petitions.
Mandates were supervised by the Permanent Mandates Commission with less direct access.
blocks.answer: Clear aim of self-rule and stronger supervision.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Role of visiting missions
blocks.statement: Explain how UN visiting missions helped Cameroonians.
steps: Missions visited the territories and reported on conditions.
Petitions allowed individuals and groups to raise concerns.
UN debates kept the question of the territories’ future on the international agenda.
blocks.answer: A channel for opinions and international attention.
